question: One week after delivery, a 3550-g (7-lb 13-oz) newborn has multiple episodes of bilious vomiting and abdominal distention. He passed urine 14 hours after delivery and had his first bowel movement 3 days after delivery. He was born at term to a 31-year-old woman. Pregnancy was uncomplicated and the mother received adequate prenatal care. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 132/min, and respirations are 50/min. Examination shows a distended abdomen. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. Digital rectal examination shows a patent anus and an empty rectum. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the abdomen is shown. Which of the following is the underlying cause of these findings?

options.opa: Defective migration of neural crest cells
options.opb: Disruption of blood flow to the fetal jejunum
options.ope: Failed recanalization of the fetal duodenum

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Defective migration of neural crest cells" -> "absence of ganglion cells in colon" -> "lack of peristalsis" -> "intestinal obstruction" -> "bilious vomiting" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Disruption of blood flow to the fetal jejunum" -> "intestinal atresia" -> "obstruction" -> "bilious vomiting" -> "abdominal distention" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Mutation in the CFTR gene" -> "thickened secretions" -> "meconium ileus" -> "intestinal obstruction" -> "bilious vomiting" -> 75%
CHAIN: "Abnormal rotation of the intestine" -> "malrotation" -> "volvulus" -> "intestinal obstruction" -> "bilious vomiting" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Failed recanalization of the fetal duodenum" -> "duodenal atresia" -> "intestinal obstruction" -> "bilious vomiting" -> "abdominal distention" -> 90%
enhanced_information: The clinical presentation of bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, delayed passage of meconium, and an empty rectum on digital examination in a newborn is most consistent with Hirschsprung disease. This condition is caused by defective migration of neural crest cells, leading to an absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon, resulting in a lack of peristalsis and subsequent intestinal obstruction. The retrieved evidence path 'Neural Crest Cell-INTERACTS_WITH->(Genes)-PART_OF->(Colon)' supports this mechanism. Other options, such as intestinal atresia, meconium ileus, intestinal malrotation, and duodenal atresia, are less likely given the specific clinical findings. For instance, duodenal atresia typically presents earlier and with a 'double bubble' sign on x-ray, which is not mentioned here. Therefore, the underlying cause of the findings is best explained by defective migration of neural crest cells, leading to Hirschsprung disease.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the newborn, including delayed passage of meconium, abdominal distention, and bilious vomiting, is suggestive of Hirschsprung disease. This condition is caused by a defective migration of neural crest cells, leading to an absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon, resulting in a functional obstruction. The empty rectum on digital examination further supports this diagnosis. The other options, such as disruption of blood flow, CFTR mutation, abnormal rotation, and failed recanalization, are less consistent with the described symptoms and findings.
